meta.title: Agentic Coding is Burning Me Out
meta.author: deejayy

comments.author: mattgreenrocks
comments.text:
Gonna be that guy and say…stop doing it if it hurts? There are ways to use AI without burning yourself out.

Ceding agency to industry hype is a choice you make.

comments.author: zk
comments.text: Yeah this is usually my response to these kinds of posts... All the problems often seem really obviously self-inflicted to me, an outsider to the LLM hype.

comments.author: fleebee
comments.text:
The LLMs are currently generating so many orders of magnitude more code than any single human could ever have the chance to properly debug or reason through. You find yourself signing off on an overwhelming amount of raw code just to keep up with the output that's expected these days.


I'm not sure I like this fantasytrend of pumping out so much software so fast that no human can reason about how it works.


A lot of ambitious engineers think they just need to spin up more agents and ship more code so they can outwork everyone else, but MOAR is probably not the answer.


Yes, exactly! Slow down to think about the utility of whatever you're creat--


Better review and verification loops sound like the obvious answer, but you have to figure out who is actually going to build them, you or the LLM.


...right. Just throw more LLMs at the problem, and maybe it goes away.

comments.author: xantronix
comments.text:
When the ability to produce such volumes of code at such speeds becomes commonplace and apparently expected, nothing good happens in the long term. The sad thing is, we won't know the full toll of this raw expedience, and the pressures forcing this stuff into being, for some time yet. The cracks are showing, as evidenced by the author's experiences, but even telling these stories seems to require a fair degree of bravery since this would counter the dominant narrative keeping the money flowing.

People are growing more tired as they are expected to produce mindbogglingly more than they ever had. They grow tired of seeing their friends laid off. They grow tired of feeling numbed by too much high level interaction with an LLM agent and too little interaction with the physical systems beneath. They grow tired of a lack of direction and meaning: What does this bounty, or rather, excess, bring us? Who benefits the most?

Plates will fall.

comments.author: strugee
comments.text:
I've found it helpful to use LLMs to do mechanical work that I've already mentally defined. If I'm trying to understand a problem space at the same time as I'm trying to review the LLM output, that's where I start to get into the unpleasant experiences this post is talking about.

Often, your understanding of a problem changes as you work through it, and therefore the final design changes too. This means that in order for me to use an LLM as described above, definitionally it needs to be for a problem that not only do I understand well, but probably one that I've done before in some shape. That way I can be confident not only that I could solve it myself (I'm competent in the problem space), but also that I can fully anticipate those design lessons that would normally come up in the middle (I fully understand the problem space).

I think we're used to thinking of "this problem is solveable" as the former, but with LLMs, you're going to have a bad time unless you set the (much) higher standard of the latter.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text: People following poor software development practices which produce reams of code to do nothing are doing it faster than ever before.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
This piece captures the current tension around agentic engineering really well.

We can generate working, tested, documented, and maybe correctly designed code much faster than before.

We still need to spend significant cognitive bandwidth undertaking and reasoning about what we've built, and verifying that it does the right things in the right ways.

I expect it's going to take quite a while to figure out the new sustainable shape of software development with these tools. The coding agents only got good in
November so this problem is still only very thinly explored.

comments.author: strugee
comments.text:

Genuinely curious for your take - how do you expect general availability of Mythos-class models to affect the problem space?

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
It looks like GPT-5.5 - which is generally available today - is similar in capabilities to Mythos.

I don't think it changes much, other than security holes being a little bit easier to find. I'm hoping that the Firefox CTO's take holds up, that this is a big advantage for defenders.

If you assume that the number of vulnerabilities present in a piece of software is finite then that should work out.

comments.author: srcreigh
comments.text: Thanks for sharing that Mozilla article. It's fascinating that the author feels as if they are able to fix every defect. Of course, any new release of any code could have new vulnerabilities. I hope we don't end up in a world where only the rich can make secure code.

comments.author: evert
comments.text:
I think quality in a lot of software development has always been about finding 'whatever the user can bare' ever since were able to update over the internet.

Whenever people talk about this software quality crisis I can't help but wonder where they have been the last 15 years.

I appreciate all that consider this a craft and want to be proud of the thing they ship,  but it feels almost contrarian.

So I carefully sculpt my personal projects at home and crank out 100s of lines of code per day at work, and the situation at work will not change until the bottom line is affected by it.

Hated it at first but it's also made me less emotional about my work which has some work/life benefits as well.

comments.author: lacker
comments.text: This reminds me of something that often happens to new managers. You try to keep handling all the code that 10 people are writing the same way you would handle you own, and it doesn't scale. You have to figure out what can be delegated and what can't. It's a real skill though that has to be learned.

comments.author: zem
comments.text: for me the sweet spot of using an LLM to write code is figuring out what smallish piece of code I would implement next if I were doing it by hand, and have the LLM do that. the resulting diff is both small enough to review manually, and familiar enough because I have spent a few minutes visualising what it should be, and if the agent has not done it in the way that I would I can prompt it to refine the code or just fix it up myself. overall it saves a bit of tedium and I don't feel overwhelmed by trying to keep up with an AI firehose.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
I hit a wall with AI Coding late 2025. I was running 6-10 terminals with agents in parallel. The cognitive/switching load with this is really high.

It was pretty much at that stage that I realized something needed to change: Probably half my time is spent uplifting my own agentic tools/workflow. The other half feeding + watering.

It was a big shift, but I've got to say, I'm less stressed now than I was when I was coding by hand.

comments.author: stig
comments.text:
I have noticed similar issues. I’m busier than ever during the day, and more tired than before at the end of the day.

In Slow Productivity Cal Newport says:


Do fewer things. Work at a natural pace. Obsess over quality.


I’m trying to follow that. It’s hard for me, the first in particular, but I’m less tired and more satisfied with work when I manage to follow it.

I do sometimes have several agents running at once, but typically for adversarial review of the main problem, or smaller issues like helping me research a question from a colleague, prepare for a meeting, or review team mates’ pull requests.
